analysis.one_liner: Requires private equity to get federal licenses to buy health care businesses and disclose finances and political spending.
analysis.headline: Backed by 9 of 100 senators, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on July 25, 2024 and died there without a hearing, markup, or vote when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require private equity-controlled corporations to obtain a license from the Department of Health and Human Services before buying or investing in hospitals, nursing homes, physician practices, and other health care entities. It would also make for-profit health care owners report their debts, fees, staffing levels, wage cuts, and political spending to HHS, with the data made public. Other provisions would require hospitals to give 90 days' notice before closing or cutting services, block sale-leaseback deals with real estate trusts that would weaken a hospital's finances, bar investment companies from stripping assets out of health care businesses, and put pension obligations first in health care bankruptcies.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients in communities served by private-equity-owned or other for-profit health facilities, through licensing, transparency, and rules meant to prevent sudden closures, understaffing, and asset-stripping. Health workers gain reporting on wage cuts, staffing ratios, and labor-law violations, and pension plan members gain priority for withdrawal liability in health care bankruptcies. Community health centers and the National Health Service Corps would be funded by license fees and penalties.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients, health workers, and pension plan members

how_it_helps.text: Private equity firms would need an HHS license before purchasing or investing in a health care entity, and HHS could deny or revoke licenses for price gouging, understaffing, or access barriers — with revocation forcing the firm to divest its health care holdings.

For-profit owners of health care entities would have to report debts, debt-to-equity ratios, fees collected by private equity funds, dividends, staffing levels and staff-to-patient ratios, wage and benefit reductions, labor-law complaints, facility closures, and all political spending — with the data posted publicly and audited.

HHS could require private-equity-controlled firms to set up escrow accounts covering at least five years of operating and capital costs, so staff and nearby community providers are paid if a facility closes or cuts essential services.

Hospitals would have to notify HHS at least 90 days before closing or discontinuing services, submit a public mitigation plan, submit to a 45-day public comment period, and face penalties including up to a three-year ban on Medicare enrollment for violations.

Sale-leaseback deals with real estate investment trusts that would weaken a hospital's finances would be prohibited, health care rents would no longer count toward REIT tax status, investment companies would be barred from stripping assets from health care entities, and bankruptcy courts would have to prioritize pension withdrawal liability and weigh regional access to care in health care bankruptcies.
License application fees and penalties would fund the National Health Service Corps, community health centers, teaching health centers, and hospitals serving low-income patients.

analysis.who_pays: Private equity funds, for-profit health care owners, and health care REITs would bear the direct costs: license fees, five-year escrow requirements, extensive financial and political-spending disclosure, and divestment if licenses are revoked. Registered investment companies would lose the ability to strip assets from health care entities. Some compliance costs could be passed on through higher prices or reduced investment in struggling facilities.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity and health care REITs

drawbacks.text: The licensing and escrow requirements are blunt: requiring five years of operating and capital expenditures in escrow, plus a government license for any acquisition, could slow or block capital from reaching struggling hospitals and nursing homes that some investors would otherwise keep open — the strongest good-faith objection to the bill.

The bill gives the HHS Secretary very broad discretion — licenses can be denied for 'such other metrics as the Secretary determines appropriate,' and a research provision contemplates a future total ban on for-profit ownership of health care entities — which concentrates enormous gatekeeping power in one executive agency and would invite legal challenges.

The reporting burden is wide: it applies not only to private equity but to any for-profit corporation owning or affiliated with a hospital, physician practice, nursing home, hospice, or other Medicare-enrolled provider, requiring ten years of detailed financial data and disclosure of executives' salaries and political spending.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The transparency, closure-notice, and bankruptcy-priority provisions promise clear benefits for patients and workers at a moderate compliance cost, and disclosure of political spending by health care owners sheds light on influence over Congress. The licensing, escrow, and REIT provisions are far more aggressive: they could genuinely protect communities from extractive ownership, but they could also slow investment in facilities that depend on outside capital, and the bill relies on sweeping, discretionary HHS authority rather than narrow rules. On balance a strong patient-protection bill whose bluntest tools carry real trade-offs an honest supporter should acknowledge.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate in late July 2024 and sent to the Finance Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it, so it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Markey introduced the Health Over Wealth Act on July 25, 2024, joined by eight cosponsors — seven Senate Democrats and one Independent — with a stated focus on private equity ownership of health care.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day. That was the last action of any kind: no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor vote ever followed.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill expired in committee — none of its licensing, disclosure, closure-notice, REIT, or bankruptcy provisions ever took effect.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private equity funds, for-profit health care owners, and health care REITs are better off: none of the new licensing, disclosure, escrow, closure-notice, or tax rules were ever enacted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity and health care REITs

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken, so no partisan split shows up in the record; support was entirely Democratic-plus-one-Independent (9 senators), with no Republican cosponsors and no recorded opposition.

industries.note: The bill would require HHS licenses to buy or invest in health care entities, mandate disclosure of fund fees, debts, and political spending, allow forced escrow of five years of costs, and allow revocation of licenses with forced divestment — while directing research toward a potential total ban on private equity ownership of health care.

industries.industry: Health care real estate investment trusts (REITs)
industries.note: Sale-leaseback deals that would weaken a hospital's finances would be banned, and rent from health care properties would no longer count toward REIT tax status, reducing the tax advantages of owning hospital real estate.

industries.industry: For-profit hospital, nursing home, and physician practice chains
industries.note: Owners would face extensive financial, staffing, wage, and political-spending reporting, 90-day notice plus mitigation plans before closing or cutting services, and penalties up to a three-year Medicare enrollment ban — costs, but rules that also apply to owners that keep facilities open and staffed.
The Investment Company Act would be amended to make it unlawful for a registered investment company to strip an asset from a health care entity or undermine care quality or access.

industries.industry: Community health centers and safety-net health workforce programs
industries.note: License fees and civil penalties would be dedicated to the National Health Service Corps, community health centers, teaching health centers, and hospitals serving disproportionate shares of low-income patients.
